newsitem.title: USA: US House chair sees flaws in Clinton plan for D.C.
newsitem.headline: US House chair sees flaws in Clinton plan for D.C.

text.p: A key U.S. House panel chairman said on Tuesday that the White House's revitalization plan for the District of Columbia does not provide enough tax relief and economic development options for the city.

"Many groups with credible background in regional issues believe that the administration's proposals do not fully address concerns about tax relief and economic development," U.S. Rep. Thomas Davis (R-Va.), chairman of the House Government Reform Committee's subpanel on D.C., said.

"I share those concerns and expect that this subcomittee will shortly begin to translate many of these ideas into a concrete legislative initiative," Davis added in opening remarks at the panel's fourth hearing on Clinton's proposed National Capital Revitalization and Self-Government Plan.

The administration on January 14 announced a $3.9 billion, five-year revitalization plan for the District that would end the $3.56 billion federal payment Congress would have made to the city over that period. The plan is estimated to save D.C. roughly $770 million over that period.

Davis said many studies of the D.C. economy "make the point quite well that lowering taxes may be the only way to bring the District back. It is local taxes and fees which are disprportionately high and cause people and businesses to leave or never start in the District," he said.

Stephen Fuller, a public policy professor at George Mason University, called Clinton's plan a "significant step" for the city. But he said Clinton's proposal to end the city's annual federal payment "flawed."

Roger Blunt, co-chair of The Greater Washington Board of Trade, also applauded Clinton's plan. But he added, "While the federal government's assumption of many state-like functions is an important change, we are not yet convinced that changing these roles warrants elimination of the federal payment," he said.
